_comment: What price a ticket actually opens at - the one number every stop on
that ticket is measured from.
market buy   -> the ask (it crosses the spread)
market sell  -> the bid
limit / stop -> the resting price that was asked for
Python: aurion.runtime.risk.market_entry, used by Trader when it sizes
and caps an order. JavaScript: marketEntry / ticketEntry in app.js, used
by the risk line under the ticket.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. The desk measured a market order's stop from the
MID - a price nobody trades at. The engine fills at bid/ask, so the desk
understated the cost of every market stop by half the spread, on both
sides, always in the direction that looks safer than it is:
EURUSD  0.00002 spread,  200-tick stop, 1 lot:  199.00 vs 200.00   -0.5%
US30    4.0     spread,   50-tick stop, 1 lot:   48.00 vs  50.00   -4.0%
BTCUSD  12.0    spread, 5000-tick stop, 1 lot:   44.00 vs  50.00  -12.0%
XAUUSD  0.30    spread,  100-tick stop, 1 lot:   85.00 vs 100.00  -15.0%
A trader working to a 100 cap would set a stop the desk priced at 100,
the engine would price the same stop at 118 and pull it in to fit, and
the stop that reached the broker was not the stop that was agreed to.
Adding a case here is how the rule changes, and it must then pass on
both sides.

market.why: a buy crosses the spread and fills at the ask
a sell fills at the bid
a wide spread is where the two readings diverge most
and on the sell side of the same quote
case does not decide a fill price
an unknown side has no entry - it must not silently become the mid
nor does a close or a cancel name a fill price
no ask means no buy price, rather than a guess
no bid means no sell price
junk in the quote is not a price

_implied_comment: Which side a half-filled ticket is for. The desk needs this because
buy and sell are only chosen when the button is pressed, while the risk
line has to be drawn as the stop is being typed. The stop says it: a
stop below the market protects a long, a stop above it protects a short.
A take profit says the same thing the other way round.
This one is desk-only - the engine is always told the side - so it is
exercised from the JavaScript side alone.

implied.why: a stop below the market is protecting a long
a stop above it is protecting a short
a target above the market is a long
a target below it is a short
both set and agreeing - a long
both set and agreeing - a short
both below the market is a broken ticket, not a guess
no market price means no reading
a stop exactly at the market is not a side
